--- subtitle: what data is available and where it comes from description: | - SAP BI extracts serve as the foundation: article, customer, sales & forecast data - Data was scoped to finished goods under Make-to-Stock with ambient storage - The modeling dataset is based on the top-performing MSO and A-class articles - Exploratory analysis confirmed temporal seasonality and product hierarchy depth - Data quality is high overall, with minimal missing values and no major outliers number-sections: false toc: true # show page‐TOC (right‐sidebar) on _every_ page toc-depth: 3 # include ## and ### in the TOC --- # Data Understanding {#sec-02-data-understanding} ::: {.cell} ::: ## Identification of Data Sources {#sec-02-identification} Table @tbl-02-data-sources summarizes the data sources used in this project, detailing their type, time span, granularity, system of record (SoR), and content. All data is sourced from SAP BI, which extracts it from the underlying systems of record. The table also lists the specific SAP tables used for each data source. ::: {#tbl-02-data-sources} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Data Source Type Time-Span Granularity SoR Table Content

customer MD SAP S4 KNVV customer attr. hierachy
sales TD > 2020 daily SAP S4 LIPS customer orders + free-of-charge
forecasts TD > 2023 monhtly QAD monthly pre- & post Demand review forecasts
````` ::: ::: Overview of data sources used in the project\ MD = Master Data, TD = Transaction Data ::: ### Articles {#sec-02-articles} The Article Master Data is extracted from `MARC` which contains Plant specific data, this is enhanced with sales organization specific data from `MVKE` and global article data from `MARA`, applied filters are shown in Table @tbl-02-data-sources-article-filters. ::: {#tbl-02-data-sources-article-filters} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

MARC-PERKZ W only Ambient
````` ::: ::: Article Master Data Filters\ see @sec-01-bu-scope for reasons for article-filters. ::: ### Customers {#sec-02-customers} Customer Master Data is sourced from `KNVV`, which contains sales-organization-specific information, and is enriched with global attributes from `KNA1`. This includes customer classification fields such as type (e.g., internal, external, one-time customer, or employee). Customers flagged as employees are excluded from the analysis. ### Sales {#sec-02-sales} Sales data is extracted from `LIPS`, which contains delivery records. Only completed deliveries which are goods-issued are taken into account. Table @tbl-02-data-sources-sales-filters shows the applied filters to select standard sales orders and free-of-charge orders. ::: {#tbl-02-data-sources-sales-filters .table} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Sales Data Filters
Document Type Item Category Reason
TA TAN; ZTAQ; YGF1 standard sales orders
KB; ZDR standard sales orders
TA TANN; ZTNG free-of-charge orders
KL; ZFD free-of-charge orders
````` ::: ::: Sales data filters ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Fixed Planned Promotions are excluded"} Articles flagged in the Article Master data as Fixed Planned Promotions are excluded because they aren’t forecasted—instead, they’re delivered by contract and thus always achieve 100 % forecast accuracy. ::: ### Forecasts {#sec-02-forecasts} Forecasts are generated monthly for each article–plant–customer combination, with a planning horizon of up to three years. For this research, the focus is on the year 2024, using a forecast horizon of up to 12 months. Consequently, only forecasts generated from 2023 onward are considered, see @fig-05-cv for visual illustration. Since forecasts are created both before and after the Demand Review, the dataset is split into two versions: *pre-Demand Review* and *post-Demand Review*. The pre-Demand Review forecasts are used for the initial analysis, while the post-Demand Review forecasts serve as the basis for final validation. ## Data Collection Report {#sec-02-data-collection} Table @tbl-02-data-collection summarizes the data collection process, including the data sources, types, extraction dates, record counts, file sizes, and keys used for each data set. The data is collected from the SAP system and stored in a structured format for further processing. Pre- and post-Demand Review forecasts are stored as separate files, one for each month in which they were created. Roughly: - each Family contains roughly 5 customers - each Account contains roughly 2 sold-to parties - each Key Account contains roughly 3 accounts, ::: {#tbl-02-data-description-hierarchy-customer .table} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Summary: Customer Hierachy ::: ### Time Series Patterns {#sec-02-data-exploration-time-series} Certainly! Here's a rephrased version with a clearer emphasis on seasonal and trend patterns that exponential smoothing (ETS) and Box-Jenkins (ARMA/ARIMA) methods can exploit: **Exploiting Temporal Structure for Forecasting** Time series forecasting is most effective when the data exhibits temporal structure—patterns over time that models can learn and project forward. Two key components of this structure are **trend** (long-term directional movement) and **seasonality** (recurring cycles, such as weekly demand spikes or annual holiday effects). Methods like **exponential smoothing (ETS)** are particularly suited to capture and extrapolate trend and seasonal components through adaptive smoothing techniques. Similarly, **Box-Jenkins models**—including **ARMA** and **ARIMA**—leverage autocorrelation structures in the data, modeling dependencies between past and future values to make informed predictions. When such temporal patterns are present, these models can generate meaningful forecasts by systematically exploiting the underlying structure. In contrast, when a series lacks trend, seasonality, or autocorrelation—essentially behaving like random noise—forecasting yields little more than projecting the mean or last known value. Thus, effective forecasting depends on the assumption that past behavior offers useful insight into future outcomes. Figure @fig-02-seasonal_trend_strength_facet_plot displays the strength of seasonality (y-axis) and trend (x-axis) for each combination of material and customer hierarchy levels. Notably, all levels exhibit clear seasonality (values \> 0.64) and a meaningful trend component (values \> 0.5), indicating a strong temporal structure—an encouraging sign for effective forecasting. ::: {#fig-02-seasonal_trend_strength_facet_plot .figure} ![](../images/seasonal_trend_strength_facet_plot.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} igure @fig-02-examples_facet_plot presents examples from various hierarchy levels that exhibit strong seasonality along with noticeable trend components. ::: ::: {#fig-02-examples_facet_plot .figure} ![](../images/examples_facet_plot.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} ::: ### Forecastability {#sec-02-data-exploration-forecastability} #### ABC/XYZ Classification {#sec-02-data-exploration-abc} The ABC/XYZ classification is a commonly used framework for prioritizing items based on their business impact and forecastability. It supports decision-making on which items warrant detailed forecasting and tighter control. - ABC: Does the item have sufficient importance to justify close monitoring or forecasting? - XYZ: Is the item predictable enough to produce reliable forecasts? ::: {#fig-02-abc-xyz .figure} ![](../images/ABCXYZ.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} - AX: High-priority & stable items, forecast carefully. - AZ: High-priority & erratic items, forecast with caution. - CZ: Low-priority & erratic items: Maybe don’t forecast. ::: #### Syntetos-Boylan (SB) Classification {#sec-02-data-exploration-sb} The Syntetos–Boylan (SB) classification extends the ABC/XYZ framework by integrating demand variability and forecastability. It provides a more nuanced understanding of demand patterns and supports the selection of suitable forecasting methods, see [@syntetos2005categorization]. For BioBalance, the time series data is predominantly a mix of intermittent and smooth demand, with the specific pattern varying by the level of aggregation. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
SB_Type Best_fit_Methods
Smooth SES; Holt’s; Holt-Winters (Triple Exp); ARIMA; Moving Average
Erratic Damped exponential; Holt-Winters (if seasonal); ARIMA with volatility modeling
Intermittent Croston; SBA; TSB; bootstrapped quantile models
Lumpy Croston variants + heuristics; simulation; judgmental overlays
````` ::: ::: Sufficient Historical Data and Pattern Stability Reliable demand classification and effective forecasting require an adequate historical record—ideally covering multiple seasonal cycles and enough observations to separate meaningful patterns from random noise. For instance, capturing annual seasonality in monthly data typically requires at least 2–3 years of history. In our analysis, SB-class distributions appear stable over time, aside from fluctuations near the lower boundary—particularly in the first few months, where the classification is less reliable due to insufficient data. As such, early observations (less than 6 months) are omitted from interpretation. Encouragingly, as time series length increases, the proportion of smooth demand series rises. This shift is favorable for forecast accuracy, as smooth series are more predictable and well-suited to traditional forecasting methods, see figure @fig-02-plot_sbc_by_ts ::: {#fig-02-plot_sbc_by_ts .figure} ![](../images/plot_sbc_by_ts.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} ::: Figure @fig-02-plot_sbm illustrates the distribution of SB-class types across different aggregation levels, highlighting the prevalence of smooth and intermittent demand patterns. The chart shows that as the aggregation level increases, the proportion of smooth demand series also increases, while intermittent demand remains significant. THis plot is made at the aggregation level ProdCat-Channel. The complete analysis for all aggregation levels is available in @fig-02-SBCSIEL. ::: {#fig-02-plot_sbm .figure} ![](../images/plot_sbm.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} ::: **Model Implications:** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Method Assumes Handles Fit_in_SB_Classification Notes
Moving Average Stationarity; no trend or seasonality Smooth to moderate variability 'Smooth; maybe Erratic' Simple; not suitable for intermittent or seasonal
Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) Stationary; no trend or seasonality Random variation; no trend/season 'Smooth' Cannot handle trend or seasonality
Double Exponential Smoothing Linear trend Trend 'Smooth; Erratic' Better than SES for trending series
Triple Exponential Smoothing (Holt-Winters) Trend + seasonality Seasonality 'Smooth; some Erratic' Not appropriate for intermittent/lumpy
ARIMA / ARMA Stationarity (or with differencing) Trend + autocorrelation 'Smooth; Erratic' Requires regular frequency and sufficient data
Croston / SBA / TSB Zero-heavy demand Intermittency 'Intermittent; Lumpy' Designed specifically for intermittent demand
````` ::: ::: The distribution of SB-class types across different aggregation levels is shown in figure @fig-02-SBCSIEL. Note the high level of smooth time series, especially for the weighted percentage which takes the sales volume into account. This indicates that the majority of sales are driven by smooth demand patterns, which are more predictable and suitable for traditional forecasting methods. ::: {#fig-02-SBCSIEL .figure} ![](../images/SBCSIEL.png){fig-align="left" width="15cm"} Weighted SB-Classification (S, I, E, L) for each aggregation level ::: #### ABC/XYZ versus Syntetos-Boylan (SB) Classification {#sec-02-data-exploration-abc-sb} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Aspect XYZ ADI_CV2_Syntetos_Boylan
Metric Coefficient of Variation (CV) ADI + CV² (more granular)
Forecastability Measures volatility Measures both volatility and intermittency
Use case Broad segmentation for policy setting Model selection and demand type understanding
Z class equivalent Often aligns with 'Lumpy' or 'Erratic' Differentiates between those
````` ::: ::: [details and coding on data_understanding](../coding/21_data_understanding.html) ## Data Quality Report {#sec-02-data-quality} ### Data Quality Assessment {#sec-02-data-quality-assessment} all 0 duplicates, zero quantity, unexpected NAs **Actions taken:** ## Summary of Data Understanding {#sec-02-summary} - The dataset combines master and transactional data from SAP BI and QAD systems. - Sales and forecasts are scoped to a single MSO and A-class finished goods. - Product and customer hierarchies follow a consistent four-level structure. - Exploratory analysis confirms sufficient data volume, patterns, and quality. - The data is now ready for scoping, transformation, and modeling.
